path.title: The Science of Well-Being
path.subtitle: Build happiness with evidence, not vibes
path.summary: Most people chase happiness the way a labrador chases its tail; lots of motion, lots of belief, no actual progress. This path hands you the psychology behind why your gut is wrong about happiness, and the tiny, measurable habits that move the needle. By the end you can diagnose your own well-being and run a 14-day experiment that actually changes the number.

lessons.title: Why You Want the Wrong Things
lessons.subtitle: Your brain is a wedding photographer with no memory card

audioChapters.label: Opening — your brain is a bad GPS

blocks.md:
You think you know what will make you happy. You are usually wrong. Not in a charming, philosophical way; wrong in a measurable, repeatable, fund-the-research way.

The mistake follows patterns, and once you see the patterns, you cannot unsee them. By the end of this lesson you will be able to look at your own *want list* and tell which items are signal and which are noise. Welcome to the most expensive bug in your operating system.

blocks.title: Mental model: the wedding photographer with a broken memory card
blocks.md: Think of your brain as a wedding photographer with a card that only saves the *peak* and the *end* of every event. It then forecasts the future based on those two frames — and confidently tells you the trip will feel a certain way, the meeting will be excruciating, the new job will be life-changing. **The forecasts are systematically wrong, in a direction we can predict.**

blocks.caption: The brain camera in motion — watch the photographer drop frames in real time.

hi-IN.title: Apna analogy — Mahindra Thar wala
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, scene yeh hai. Tu Mahindra Thar le aaya. Pehle 14 din — society mein hero. Caretaker bhi salute marta hai. Day 30 — *gaadi*. Day 60 — parking ka issue. Day 90 — "yaar Defender lena chahiye tha."

Thar nahi badla. Tu adapt ho gaya. Aur ab tujhe Defender chahiye — same loop, bigger EMI.

en.title: Same point, no cricket
en.md: You buy the dream car. Two weeks of hero status with the parking guard. Two months later it's just "the car." Three months later you're researching the next one. The car didn't change. Your camera adapted.

blocks.md:
**Miswanting** is wanting things that, on arrival, do not move you the way you predicted. The term was coined by Gilbert and Wilson; verified across decades on lottery winners, salary jumps, and yes, breakups.

A crisp number: a ₹20 lakh salary jump produces an 8 to 12 week happiness spike. After that, satisfaction returns to baseline while the new EMI does not.

blocks.title: What miswanting actually looks like over 90 days after a salary jump

steps.label: Day 0 — The Want
steps.body: You imagine the new salary, see yourself in a calmer apartment, sleeping deeper, finally relaxed. Predicted mood: 9 out of 10, permanent.

steps.label: Day 3 — The Bump
steps.body: Offer accepted. You text seven people. Your dopamine has, briefly, the chemistry of a small lottery win. Real mood: 8 out of 10.

steps.label: Day 21 — The New Normal
steps.body: You stop noticing the salary. You start noticing your manager's tone in standups. Mood: 7.4 out of 10.

steps.label: Day 60 — The Comparison Reset
steps.body: You learn what your peer at the next company makes. You feel poorer than you did three months ago, on a higher salary. Mood: 6.9 out of 10.

steps.label: Day 90 — Baseline
steps.body: Same mood as before, slightly more tax, more meetings. The thing you wanted did exactly what the data said it would do. Mood: 7.0 out of 10.

blocks.prompt: What is miswanting?

choices.label: Wanting things that do not increase long-term happiness as predicted
choices.explain: Correct. Miswanting is about a faulty *prediction*, not a faulty desire.

choices.label: Wanting fewer things than you should
choices.explain: Tempting because minimalism is in the air, but no — miswanting is about accuracy of forecasts, not quantity of stuff.

choices.label: Wanting things you cannot afford
choices.explain: Did not read carefully. Affordability is not the issue; the issue is that even when you get the thing, it does not feel the way you imagined.

choices.label: Not knowing what you want
choices.explain: Different bug. Miswanting is when you know exactly what you want, get it, and find out the future-you did not actually need it.

hi-IN.title: Shaadi se pehle vs shaadi ke baad — classic miswant
hi-IN.md:
**Shaadi se pehle:** "Bas shaadi ho jaaye, life set hai."
**Shaadi ke 90 din baad:** "Ration kaun laayega? Maid kab aayegi? Mummy ka call kaun uthayega?"

Shaadi ka problem nahi hai. Prediction ka problem hai. Tera dimaag ne *bridal photoshoot* save ki, *Tuesday evening grocery* skip kar diya. Aur ab woh Tuesday tujhe roz milta hai.

en.title: Pre-event vs post-event prediction error
en.md: Before any major life event your brain saves the highlight reel. After the event, you live in the parts the brain skipped — Tuesday evening grocery, the unloading, the small recurring negotiations. The event isn't the problem; the forecast was.

blocks.md:
The **arrival fallacy** is miswanting with a finish line. *"Once I crack the JEE, life starts."* *"Once I hit FIRE, I will relax."* *"Once the wedding is over, we will breathe."*

Tal Ben-Shahar named it after winning his own squash championship: he won, expected ecstasy, got about 11 minutes of it, then went looking for the next finish line. **The brain treats arrival as a *transition*, not a *destination*.** And the second your foot crosses the line, your brain quietly installs the next one.

blocks.alt: A staircase climbing up. Each step has a flag at the top labelled 'finish line.' As you reach each flag, the next one materializes higher up.
blocks.caption: Every finish line is the starting point of the next one. The staircase is infinite by design.

coach.name: Bhai-GPT
coach.role: Your friend who reads psychology papers between cigarettes

intro: Oye. Welcome to the Want Audit. 👋
Main tujhe paanch real-life wants dikhaunga. Tu bata — yeh **legit want** hai (worth chasing), **miswant** hai (prediction error), ya **depends** hai (need more info)?
Don't stress. Half the population gets these wrong. The other half is lying.

scenarios.situation: Aarav, 28, software engineer. "Once I get the iPhone 16 Pro Max, I'll feel ahead in life."
scenarios.explain: Pure miswant. Phone bumps mood for ~14 days; "ahead in life" is a comparison-game which has no winner. Money will be gone, position unchanged.

scenarios.situation: Priya, 31, marketing manager. "Once I get the promotion, I will finally relax on weekends."
scenarios.explain: Classic arrival fallacy. Promotions almost always increase weekend work, not decrease it. The 'relax on weekends' part is doing the heavy lifting in this fantasy, and it's lying.

scenarios.situation: Rohan, 35, lawyer. "I want to fix my sleep. I'll go to bed at 11, no phone after 10:30, for 30 days straight."
scenarios.explain: Legit. Sleep is one of the few inputs that the well-being literature *consistently* finds non-fading. The plan is also specific, time-boxed, and behavioral. This is not a forecast about a feeling; it's a behavior change.

scenarios.situation: Tanya, 26, designer. "I want to move from Bangalore to Berlin because I'll be happier there."
scenarios.explain: Could go either way. If 'happier' is the prediction, suspect miswanting (place changes fade in months). If the move is for craft, community, or visa optionality, it can be a legit move. The wording is doing too much; ask her *why* she thinks she'd be happier.

scenarios.situation: You. "After this course, I'll finally have my life figured out."
scenarios.explain: Sneaky little arrival fallacy with our own course. The course gives you tools; it does not flip a switch. If you finish the course expecting an enlightenment moment, you will be disappointed in 12 weeks.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the finish-line stack
blocks.md:
You do not have one arrival fallacy; you have a **queue** of them. Promotion, then house, then car, then second house, then kid's school admission, then *their* JEE. Each arrival quietly hands the baton to the next, and you mistake the running for progress.

The fix is not to stop wanting. The fix is to ask, *what does my Tuesday afternoon look like 90 days after I cross this line?* If the answer is "basically the same as today," you have caught a miswant in the wild.

blocks.prompt: Order the stages of a textbook arrival fallacy in someone who just got into a top engineering college:

items.label: Anticipation: 'Once the result is out, life starts.'
items.detail: Pre-arrival inflation; you imagine peak happiness.

items.label: The bump: 48 hours of giddy posting and parental WhatsApp forwards
items.detail: Real spike, real short.

items.label: The dip: hostel logistics, missing friends, feeling unprepared
items.detail: Reality replaces fantasy.

items.label: The pivot: 'Once I get an internship at Goldman, life starts.'
items.detail: New finish line installed; the cycle restarts.

blocks.hint: Think pre-event, event, after-shock, then the relapse.

blocks.instruction: List 3 things you currently believe will make you noticeably happier. For each, write (a) the realistic duration of the bump, and (b) what your day-to-day will look like 90 days after.
blocks.expected:
Example:
1. New phone — bump 14 days; on day 90, it is just 'the phone,' maybe a small annoyance about battery life.
2. New job — bump 8 to 12 weeks; on day 90, the meetings feel like meetings.
3. International trip — bump 2 to 4 weeks of residual glow; on day 90, you have 700 photos you have not opened.

blocks.prompt: Your friend says: 'Once we close this funding round, I will finally enjoy life again.' What's the most accurate diagnosis?

choices.label: Arrival fallacy — they have stacked 'enjoying life' on a transition that will install the next finish line within weeks
choices.explain: Correct. The funding close is real, but it's a transition, not a destination. The brain will install the next finish line (Series B, IPO, exit) within the same 8-12 week window.

choices.label: Their funding is a bad idea
choices.explain: Did not read. The funding may be excellent. The bug is in the *prediction* about what closing will do to their inner state, not in the business decision.

choices.label: They need to be more grateful
choices.explain: Tempting wellness-bro answer. Gratitude is a downstream cheat code (lesson 4); it does not address the forecasting bug here.

choices.label: Hedonic adaptation — happiness has fallen below baseline
choices.explain: Almost-right answer. Adaptation is the *post-arrival* mechanism. The arrival fallacy is the *pre-arrival* prediction error. They are siblings, not the same bug.

hi-IN.title: Mummy aunty test — finish-line stack
hi-IN.md:
**12th boards:** "Beta, IIT crack ho jaaye, set hai."
**IIT crack:** "Beta, ab MNC mein placement, set hai."
**MNC placement:** "Beta, ab US ka onsite, set hai."
**US onsite:** "Beta, ab shaadi, set hai."
**Shaadi:** "Beta, ab bachcha, set hai."
**Bachcha:** "Beta, uski 12th boards, set hai."

Loop bhi tera, finish lines bhi tere, fatigue bhi tera. Aunty bas commentator hai.

en.title: The finish-line stack at 4 generations
en.md: Every culture has its version of the finish-line stack. School, job, marriage, kids, kids' school, kids' job. Each generation hands the next a longer queue and calls it ambition. The queue is the bug, not the ambition.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The ₹4.2 Cr Anticlimax
blocks.source: A therapist in Bandra, Mumbai (anonymised, with client permission)
blocks.story:
Riya, 28, product manager at a fintech in Lower Parel. Spent 7 years and 3 months on the FIRE plan: 62 percent savings rate, two side-hustles, a colour-coded Notion dashboard updated every Sunday at 9 p.m. The number she had picked at 21 was ₹4.2 crore. The day her portfolio crossed it, March 11, 2024, she screenshotted the brokerage app, sent it to her father, made dal-chawal, and felt nothing. Not relief, not joy, not even smugness. By Tuesday she was anxious that the market would dip and undo it.

She came to me 6 weeks later because she could not stop refreshing the app. The diagnosis was textbook miswanting: she had built her entire identity around a single forecast — *crossing the number will feel like crossing the finish line of a marathon*. Brain delivered exactly what was ordered. The forecast was wrong. The number was a number.

What she had actually wanted, surfaced over 4 sessions: the Sunday ritual with her dad of comparing portfolios, the chai breaks with her side-hustle pod on Discord, the feeling of being the youngest person in every room talking compounding. She had optimised away every one of those by hitting the number early.
blocks.takeaway: The thing you forecast you'll feel is almost never the thing you'll actually feel. Audit the side-effects of the goal before you reach it, not after.

blocks.title: Aarav vs the Promotion
blocks.setup:
It's a Wednesday night. Your phone buzzes. **Aarav, 31, software engineer at a Bengaluru product company, engaged to Meera**, has messaged you on WhatsApp.

> *yaar, big news. EM role just opened up. ₹14L hike, more scope. I HAVE to go for this. it'll change everything. you in for a coffee tomorrow? need to game-plan.*

You just finished Lesson 1. Your job is not to talk him in or out of it. Your job is to run the miswanting diagnostic before he sprints.

stages.prompt: First reply. Aarav is hyped. What do you actually send back?

options.label: 'Bro do it, EM money is unreal, don't overthink.'
options.explain: You just rubber-stamped his forecast without testing it. This is the friend version of miswanting: catching the contagion instead of containing it. Tarini is shaking her head from Pune.

options.label: 'Don't take it. EM is a trap, you'll hate the meetings.'
options.explain: You replaced his forecast with your forecast. Both forecasts are guesses. The diagnostic is supposed to surface *his* data, not yours.

options.label: 'Coffee yes. Bring two things: what your Tuesday looks like in this role, and the last time a hike actually moved your mood for more than 3 weeks.'
options.explain: You just asked for a behavioural forecast (the Tuesday) and a base rate (last hike). This is exactly the affective-forecasting checklist from the lesson. Tarini approves.

options.label: 'Make a pros/cons list and send it to me.'
options.explain: Pros/cons lists are where miswants come to dress up as logic. He'll list the ₹14L and the 'scope' and call it analysis.

stages.prompt: At coffee, Aarav says: 'Last hike was 18 months ago, ₹6L bump. Felt amazing for maybe 10 days. By month 2 I was Googling the next role.' What does this data tell you?

options.label: He needs a bigger hike this time so the boost lasts longer.
options.explain: Classic dose-response error. Hedonic adaptation does not scale linearly with size. ₹14L will follow the same curve as ₹6L, just with a slightly steeper drop.

options.label: His own n=1 evidence shows hike-driven mood lifts decay in under 30 days. He's about to forecast it'll feel different this time. It won't.
options.explain: He has personal base-rate data and he's ignoring it. This is miswanting in its purest form: the forecast contradicts his own measured history.

options.label: Means the last role was wrong. EM is the right fit, this hike will stick.
options.explain: Maybe. But you have zero evidence and one strong forecast bias. You're letting him narrate his way past the data.

options.label: Doesn't matter, money is money, the math is good.
options.explain: The lesson is not 'don't take money'. The lesson is 'don't take money *because you think it'll fix your mood*'. Different decision, different inputs.

stages.prompt: Aarav describes his Tuesday as EM: 4 hours of 1:1s, 2 hours of stakeholder syncs, 1 hour of code review, no deep work. He currently codes 5 hours a day and calls it the best part of his week. Verdict?

options.label: Solid miswant. He's optimising for status and salary while deleting the activity that actually drives his daily mood. Recommend: negotiate IC track or stay.
options.explain: He just told you the load-bearing wall of his current happiness (5 hours of coding) is being knocked down. The hike pays for the demolition. This is the diagnostic working exactly as designed.

options.label: He'll grow into the meetings. Most engineers do.
options.explain: Maybe over 18 months. But the lesson is about *forecasting accuracy*. He has not forecasted this trade-off at all; he's only forecasted the bank balance.

options.label: Tell him to take it and just block 2 hours a day to code.
options.explain: Tempting. But 'I'll just protect my deep work' is the EM new-year's resolution that dies by Q2. You've patched the symptom, not surfaced the miswant.

options.label: Inconclusive, need more data.
options.explain: You have his Tuesday breakdown, his last hike's mood decay, and his stated favourite activity. That's enough. Decisiveness is part of the diagnostic.

outcomes.perfect: 9/9. You ran a clean miswanting diagnostic on a hyped friend without becoming his therapist or his cheerleader. Aarav now has data instead of a forecast. Tarini sends a thumbs up from Pune.
outcomes.good: 6-8 points. You caught the miswant but slipped into advice-mode in places. The skill is to surface his data, not substitute yours.
outcomes.learn: Under 6. You either rubber-stamped Aarav's forecast or replaced it with your own. Re-read the affective-forecasting section and try again — the goal is to test the prediction, not to vote on the decision.

points: Your brain is a wedding photographer that only saves the peak and the end frames
Miswanting is a prediction error, not a desire problem
The arrival fallacy installs a new finish line the moment you cross the old one
Bumps from external events fade in 2 to 12 weeks; nothing in the dataset disagrees
The diagnostic question is: what does my Tuesday afternoon look like 90 days after I get this thing?

blocks.prompt: Write down one finish line you are currently running toward. What is the real, hour-by-hour life you expect on the day after you cross it?

lessons.title: Why Nothing Stays Special
lessons.subtitle: The thermostat in your skull does not care about your raise

audioChapters.label: Opening — the thermostat in your skull

blocks.md:
You assume good things keep feeling good. They do not. Your brain has, hardwired into it, a happiness thermostat — and the thermostat is annoyingly competent.

This lesson is the bad news that becomes good news. Bad: nothing stays special. Good: nothing stays awful either. The same plumbing makes both true.

blocks.alt: A round thermostat dial fixed at 7. Two arrows show events pushing it up to 9 and back to 7, then down to 5 and back to 7.
blocks.caption: Your happiness thermostat. Pushes up, pushes down — but quietly resets to its setpoint. The setpoint is the variable that actually matters, and almost nothing you buy moves it.

blocks.title: Mental model: the happiness thermostat
blocks.md:
Think of happiness like a thermostat set somewhere around 7 out of 10. External events push it briefly up (new job, vacation, biryani) or briefly down (breakup, food poisoning, a passive-aggressive Slack message). The thermostat then quietly pulls it back to 7.

**This is a feature, not a bug.** If it didn't reset, your last breakup would still be running your life — and so would your first crush. The thermostat is the reason you can function at all.

blocks.caption: Animated adaptation curve: watch the bump rise, decay, and reset across 90 days for a typical purchase, vacation, and breakup.

hi-IN.title: Goa trip wala adaptation
hi-IN.md:
Goa trip se aaya. Pehla din: instagram pe 12 stories. Doosra din: 4 stories. Saatva din: "yaar Goa toh basic hai, Bali jaana chahiye."

Goa change nahi hua bhai. Tu adapt ho gaya. Aur ab Bali ki photos teri timeline hijack kar rahi hain — same loop, alag visa.

en.title: The vacation fade
en.md: Day 1 back from holiday: 12 Instagram stories. Day 2: 4. Day 7: "that place was actually mid, the next one will be the real one." The place did not change. Your thermostat did its job.

blocks.md:
Brickman's 1978 study compared lottery winners (recent) against paraplegics (recent accident) against controls. **Eighteen months later, all three groups reported similar happiness levels.** The win and the catastrophe both faded. Adaptation is not about stoicism; it is about plumbing.

A boring number: a ₹1 lakh phone increases self-reported happiness for roughly 14 days before the upgrade becomes "the phone." By month 3 it is generating *negative* affect when the battery dies.

blocks.prompt: Hedonic adaptation implies which of the following?

choices.label: Happiness levels return to a baseline after positive changes
choices.explain: Correct. The thermostat resets up.

choices.label: Happiness levels return to a baseline after negative changes
choices.explain: Correct. Same mechanism, in the other direction. This is also why most catastrophes are survivable in psychological terms.

choices.label: Happiness only fluctuates downward over time
choices.explain: Wrong direction; adaptation is symmetric, not pessimistic.

choices.label: Material purchases never produce any happiness
choices.explain: Did not read carefully. They produce happiness; the happiness just decays on a known curve.

hi-IN.title: Bharat ka biggest adaptation — AC wala scene
hi-IN.md:
Pehla week ka AC: "yaar zindagi badal gayi."

Doosra mahine ka AC: "thoda zyada cool karna chahiye."

Teesra mahine ka bill: "yaar AC band karte hain raat ko."

Chautha mahine: "AC nahi hai matlab insaan kaise rehte hain bhai??"

Tu AC ka adapt ho gaya **dono directions mein.** Pehle uska novelty fade hua, fir uska absence intolerable ho gaya. Saala plumbing.

en.title: The AC paradox
en.md: Week 1 with the new AC: 'life-changing.' Month 3 without it: 'how do humans live without one?' You adapted to having it, then re-adapted to needing it. The thermostat works in both directions, often making you worse off than where you started.

blocks.md:
If adaptation is the enemy, the cheap counter is **variety**. Five different small pleasures (coffee with a friend Tuesday, a 4 km walk Wednesday, a new playlist Thursday) consistently beat one expensive intense pleasure (a five-star dinner, once) on weekly happiness measures.

Why: each new context partially resets the adaptation clock. Your brain is bad at adapting to a moving target. **Variety is hedonic arbitrage at zero marginal cost.**

coach.name: The Thermostat Detective
coach.role: Predicts how long bumps last. Mostly right.

intro: OK detective, you have five cases. 🔍
Each is a real life event. Predict how long the happiness bump lasts before adaptation finishes the job.
Three buckets: **fades fast** (under 1 month), **fades slow** (1 to 6 months), **mostly sticks** (12+ months). Most things are in the first bucket; a few aren't.

scenarios.situation: ₹3 lakh smartwatch upgrade.
scenarios.explain: Material upgrade in a category you already had. Fades within 14-21 days; thermostat handles it cleanly.

scenarios.situation: Moving in with a partner you have a healthy relationship with, after 4 years of dating long-distance.
scenarios.explain: Daily-life relational shift. Genuine baseline change in many cases — though only if the relationship is healthy. Bad pairings have the opposite effect.

scenarios.situation: Getting a 30% raise.
scenarios.explain: Bump is real for 8-16 weeks; partial decay from comparison and lifestyle inflation. Some signal sticks if it crosses a 'security threshold' (rent + savings); above that, it fades.

scenarios.situation: A 14-day intentional gratitude practice with specific, novel, causal entries.
scenarios.explain: Behavior changes that change *what you attend to* tend to stick — they alter the input to the thermostat, not just the level.

scenarios.situation: Buying a house.
scenarios.explain: Surprisingly slow. Despite being huge financially, the daily experience adapts within 6-9 months. Identity shift adds a small permanent bump for some; for many it's the EMI that endures.

scenarios.situation: A breakup of a relationship you knew was wrong.
scenarios.explain: Negative bumps fade fastest when the break aligned with your own judgment. The data is unambiguous: the dread is worse than the aftermath.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the intensity arms race
blocks.md:
When you feel the bump fading, your instinct is to *increase the dose*. Bigger phone, fancier dinner, longer vacation. This works for about one cycle and then your hedonic budget collapses.

**Do not chase the dragon; rotate the dragons.** Variety is structurally cheaper than intensity, structurally more sustainable, and structurally more interesting. Three out of three.

blocks.prompt: Order these moves from least to most effective at slowing hedonic adaptation, based on the research:

items.label: Buy the same favorite coffee every single morning
items.detail: Almost no anti-adaptation effect; pure routine.

items.label: Buy a more expensive version of the same coffee
items.detail: Intensity arms race; very short bump.

items.label: Rotate between 4 different coffee shops on different days
items.detail: Variety; meaningful adaptation slowdown.

items.label: Skip the coffee for a week, then return to it
items.detail: Deprivation re-sensitizes the reward system; strongest single move.

blocks.instruction: Pick one daily pleasure you take for granted (coffee, your evening walk, your favorite show). Design a 7-day experiment that uses *variety or deprivation* to re-sensitize you to it. Be specific about days.
blocks.expected:
Example: I currently watch one episode of Brooklyn 99 every evening on autopilot.
Days 1–4: skip entirely; replace with reading.
Day 5: watch with full attention, no phone.
Days 6–7: rotate to two different new shows on alternating evenings.
Expected outcome: re-sensitized enjoyment of the original show on day 8, plus a small library of variety to dip into.

blocks.prompt: Brickman 1978 — what was the headline finding about lottery winners and recent paraplegics 18 months out?

choices.label: Both groups had returned to roughly similar happiness levels, comparable to controls
choices.explain: Correct. Symmetric adaptation; both extremes faded toward baseline.

choices.label: Lottery winners were dramatically happier
choices.explain: Tempting and intuitive, but the data went the other way.

choices.label: Paraplegics reported higher happiness than winners
choices.explain: The point was not that one group flipped; it was that both adapted toward baseline.

choices.label: The study was inconclusive
choices.explain: It produced one of the most cited findings in the adaptation literature.

hi-IN.title: Mummy ke haath ka khana — paradox
hi-IN.md:
Hostel jaane se pehle: "yaar mummy ke haath ka khana boring hai, daily wahi sambhar."

Hostel ke 3 mahine baad: "BHAI MUMMY KA SAMBHAR HEAVEN HAI."

Deprivation = re-sensitization. Same sambhar, different thermostat reading. Yeh science hai bhai, sentiment nahi.

en.title: The 'mom's cooking' phenomenon
en.md: You complained about your parents' cooking your entire teen years. You leave for college. Three months later, that exact same food is suddenly the most precious thing on earth. You didn't grow up. You got deprived. Same mechanism.

blocks.title: Field Notes: Three Cities, One Thermostat
blocks.source: A couples counsellor in Indiranagar, Bengaluru
blocks.story:
Vikram, 36, and Aanya, 34. DINK couple, both in tech. Came in after 11 years of marriage, exhausted. Their pattern, mapped on a whiteboard:

- 2019, Pune to Bengaluru: 'we'll be happier with better weather, better food, more friends'. Mood lifted for ~5 months. Back to baseline by Diwali.
- 2022, Bengaluru to Goa (remote phase): 'beach, slower pace, real life'. ₹38L spent on a sea-facing 3BHK. 7 weeks of bliss in the photos. By month 4 they were arguing about who forgot to call the grocery guy.
- 2024, Goa to Bengaluru: 'we miss the cafés, the energy, our people'. Mood lifted for ~3 months. By month 5, same arguments, same Sunday-night dread.

What broke them was not the third move. It was Aanya doing the math at the dining table in July: ₹1.4 crore in moving costs, brokerage, furniture write-offs, and 11 months of cumulative *real* mood improvement across all three relocations.

The thermostat resets. They had run a 5-year experiment and produced clean evidence that geography is not the lever. The relief in the room when I drew the hedonic curve on the whiteboard was the loudest data point of the session.
blocks.takeaway: If the same problem follows you across 3 cities, the city was never the variable. The thermostat travels with you.

blocks.title: Aarav, 90 Days In
blocks.setup:
It's been 3 months. Aarav took the EM role despite your coffee-shop diagnostic (your call to let him decide was the right one).

Voice note at 11:47 p.m.:

> *yaar, EM is fine. comp is great. but my Cantril ladder this morning was 6.2 — exact same number as 90 days ago before the hike. WHAT. I was sure this would put me at like an 8. Help, what's the next move from the lesson, I forget which one to run.*

You just finished Lesson 2. Time to pick a hedonic-adaptation counter-move that actually fits Aarav's situation.

stages.prompt: First, frame the data for Aarav. What do you tell him about his 6.2?

options.label: 'You're depressed bro, see someone.'
options.explain: 6.2 is not a clinical signal, it's his baseline. Pathologising adaptation is a classic over-react. Tarini frowns from Pune.

options.label: 'This is hedonic adaptation working exactly as advertised. Your set point absorbed the hike in ~90 days. Predicted by the lesson, not a bug.'
options.explain: Naming the mechanism is half the medicine. He'll stop catastrophising once he sees this is biology, not a personal failure.

options.label: 'Quit the EM role, go back to IC.'
options.explain: You're solving a hedonic-adaptation problem with a career change. That's a sledgehammer for a thermostat issue.

options.label: 'Give it more time, it'll kick in.'
options.explain: It will not 'kick in'. The lesson literally proved adaptation is the destination, not the delay. Waiting longer = more adaptation, not less.

stages.prompt: Aarav: 'Okay, mechanism named. Now what do I actually do this week?' From the lesson, you have variety, savouring, and deprivation as counter-levers. He works 9-7, no time. Pick the highest-leverage move for *his* situation.

options.label: Variety: stop ordering the same Swiggy lunch every day. Rotate 5 spots.
options.explain: Variety works but on a small surface. Lunch isn't where his adaptation is happening — comp and role are. Low-leverage move.

options.label: Deprivation: 1-week 'comp blackout' — uninstall the brokerage app, delete payslip from Notion, no compensation talk. Reintroduce on day 8 and re-rate the ladder.
options.explain: The thing he adapted to is the *visibility* of his hike (constant payslip-checking, brokerage refresh). Removing the stimulus and reintroducing it is the textbook deprivation play. Cheap, time-bound, measurable.

options.label: Savouring: write a daily journal entry about the hike.
options.explain: Journalling about a thing he's already adapted to will accelerate the adaptation, not reverse it. You're rehearsing the new normal.

options.label: Buy a bigger apartment, fresh stimulus.
options.explain: This is the Vikram-Aanya move from the field notes. Three cities later, same thermostat. Do not recommend the move that has documented n=2 failure.

stages.prompt: Day 8. Aarav reports his ladder went from 6.2 to 7.4 during the blackout, dropped back to 6.6 after he checked the brokerage. He wants to know what to take from this experiment.

options.label: Permanent rule: never check the brokerage again.
options.explain: Over-correction. The lesson is that *exposure frequency* is the lever, not exposure itself. Going from daily to monthly will likely capture most of the gain.

options.label: The blackout was placebo, ignore it.
options.explain: +1.2 ladder points then a measurable drop on re-exposure is too clean to dismiss. He just produced his own n=1 evidence for hedonic adaptation.

options.label: Set a rule: brokerage app on the 1st of each month only. Keep the deprivation-then-savour rhythm. Re-measure ladder at day 30.
options.explain: He converted a one-off experiment into a sustainable cadence and built in measurement. This is the lesson's playbook for keeping a hedonic counter-move alive past week 2.

options.label: Repeat the blackout every week.
options.explain: Over-frequent deprivation kills the contrast effect. The lever works *because* it's rare. Once a month is plenty.

outcomes.perfect: 9/9. You named the mechanism, picked the right counter-lever for Aarav's specific adaptation surface, and turned a one-off experiment into a habit with measurement. Tarini sends one (1) approving samosa emoji from Pune.
outcomes.good: 6-8. Solid diagnosis, slightly mismatched intervention. Re-check which surface Aarav has actually adapted to before picking the lever.
outcomes.learn: Under 6. You either pathologised normal adaptation or reached for moves that don't match Aarav's specific stimulus. Re-read the variety-savouring-deprivation matrix and try again.

points: Hedonic adaptation is plumbing, not philosophy; you cannot will it away
Variety beats intensity; deprivation beats variety
The intensity arms race is the most expensive way to be only briefly happier
Symmetric adaptation is also why most bad days fade faster than you fear
The strongest single re-sensitizer is short, bounded deprivation

blocks.md:
You have now read two lessons of psychology. Statistically, this changes your behavior by roughly nothing. Welcome to the most uncomfortable lesson in the course: knowledge transfer is not the same as behavior change, and the gap is the entire game.

The good news is the gap is bridgeable, mechanically, with four parts. The bad news is that *you* will skip at least one of them on the first attempt.

blocks.title: Mental model: the planner and the doer
blocks.md:
Think of your mind as two systems: the **planner** (knows the right answer, watches documentaries, has a Notion full of habits) and the **doer** (orders biryani at 11 pm).

The planner can read a hundred books on happiness without the doer ever picking up the memo. **Behavior change is the work of getting the doer to receive a single, well-formatted memo.**

hi-IN.title: Gym ka subscription = G.I. Joe Fallacy ki textbook example
hi-IN.md:
January 1: gym membership liya. Joining day photo Insta pe daala. Goggles, water bottle, headband — full setup.

January 4: "thoda thand zyada hai aaj."
January 11: "workload zyada hai, weekend mein jaaunga."
January 25: gym ka card kahaan rakha tha?
December 31: "next year se pakka."

Tujhe pata tha gym jaana hai. Knowing toh full thi. Doer ko memo nahi mila. ₹15,000 ka tuition fee — sirf ek lesson ke liye.

en.title: The gym subscription receipt
en.md: Knowing was never the bottleneck. You knew you should go to the gym. The membership card has been in your wallet since January. The doer never received the memo because nothing changed in the doer's environment. The receipt is for the lesson, not the workouts.

blocks.text: Move 1 — Name the bug: the G.I. Joe Fallacy

blocks.md:
The cartoon's tagline was *"Now you know — and knowing is half the battle."* Laurie Santos formalized the bug: in real behavior change, knowing is closer to **10%** of the battle. The other 90% is friction, cues, accountability, and environment design.

Proof you've already lived: every smoker who knows smoking is bad. Every developer who knows sleep matters. Every founder who knows they should not check email at 7 am.

Knowing is the *cheap* part. Doing is where the work, the design, and the actual life-changing happens.

blocks.title: The 4-part rewire: 'I want to walk every morning'

steps.label: 1. Cue (when + where)
steps.body: Right after the alarm rings, before checking the phone. Specific. 'Sometime in the morning' is not a cue.
steps.code:
TRIGGER: 6:30 am alarm OFF
LOCATION: bedside

steps.label: 2. Friction reduction
steps.body: Sleep in your walking clothes. Shoes by the door. Phone in another room so the doer cannot get distracted.

steps.label: 3. Tiny first step
steps.body: Goal is not 'walk 5 km.' Goal is 'put on shoes and step outside.' Once outside, the walk happens by inertia.
steps.code: TARGET: cross the doorway. That's it.

steps.label: 4. Accountability + log
steps.body: Tell one person. Tick a calendar box. The streak is the dopamine, not the walk.
steps.code: LOG: tick on physical calendar in kitchen

blocks.prompt: Why is the G.I. Joe Fallacy named what it's named?

choices.label: Because the cartoon overstated how much knowing the right answer changes behavior
choices.explain: Correct. The fallacy is in the *ratio* — knowing is a small fraction, not half.

choices.label: Because G.I. Joe was wrong about most things
choices.explain: Tempting and snarky, but no — the fallacy is specifically about the knowing/doing ratio in the tagline.

choices.label: Because behavioral psychology was invented by veterans
choices.explain: Did not read carefully. The name comes from the cartoon, not the field.

choices.label: Because the cartoon character refused to learn
choices.explain: Inverted. The character claimed knowing was enough; reality says it isn't.

hi-IN.title: Maa ka diet advice — 30 saal ka G.I. Joe Fallacy
hi-IN.md:
Maa: "beta dahi kha, raat ko paani pee, subah jaldi uth, phone band kar de."

Tujhe yeh saari information last 30 saal se hai. Ek bhi nahi follow ki. Maa galat thi? Nahi. Maa was issuing memos to the planner. Doer ne kabhi receive nahi kiya, kyunki doer ka environment kabhi nahi badla.

Doer ke saamne phone hai. Dahi nahi hai. Memo lost.

en.title: 30 years of unread memos
en.md: Your parents have been giving you the right health advice your entire life. You ignored almost all of it. They weren't wrong. They were issuing memos to the planner; the doer was somewhere else, in a different room, with a phone.

blocks.text: Move 2 — Translation moment: turn intent into a 4-part behavior

blocks.md:
The fix is mechanical, not motivational. Any behavior you actually want to install needs four parts. Drop one and the doer ignores the memo.

This is the **translation moment** of the entire course: take an English sentence ("I want to walk every morning") and translate it into a 4-part install spec the doer can actually run. Skip the translation and the planner will simply re-issue the same English sentence next January. Same EMI.

coach.name: The Habit Engineer
coach.role: Diagnoses what's missing from your last failed habit

intro: OK so you've tried this before. 🛠️
I'm going to show you four failed habits. Your job: tell me which part of the 4-part rewire was missing. **Most failures are missing only one part — that's why willpower didn't save them.**
Cue / Friction / Tiny step / Accountability. Pick the one that broke.

scenarios.situation: Rina set a goal: 'I want to read 30 minutes a day.' She intended to read 'sometime in the evening.' Books were in the bedroom drawer. She managed it 4 days the first week, 0 days the next month.
scenarios.explain: Books were accessible (low friction), 30 minutes is fine (not too tiny, but not extreme), but 'sometime in the evening' is not a cue. The doer never received a trigger. Fix: 'right after dinner, on the couch.'

scenarios.situation: Aakash: 'I'll meditate every morning.' Cue is right after brushing teeth. He has Headspace installed. The first day he set himself a 30-minute session and bailed at minute 8. Quit the app within a week.
scenarios.explain: Cue was clean, app was installed (low friction). First step was 30 minutes — way too big. Tiny first step would have been 2 minutes. Inertia would have done the rest.

scenarios.situation: Sneha: 'I'll do 20 push-ups every morning when I wake up.' She slept in her pajamas. Phone was on the bed. She has 'Tomorrow' written on a post-it. Failed all 14 days, no one ever asked her about it.
scenarios.explain: Cue is OK (waking up), friction is OK-ish (she's already awake, push-ups need no equipment), tiny step is fine (20 is small). But there is zero external accountability and the planner is fully in charge. Fix: tell one specific person, daily 👍 / 👎.

scenarios.situation: Vikram: 'I'll go to the gym after work.' Gym is 4 km away in opposite direction from home. He has to change clothes, drive 25 min through traffic, find parking, badge in. He went twice in 30 days.
scenarios.explain: Cue is fine ('after work'), tiny step is fine (just go), accountability is fine (his trainer texts him). But friction is enormous — gym is on the wrong side of his commute. Either change gym, or go *before* work, or do home workouts. Friction is the load-bearing variable here.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the willpower tax
blocks.md:
When the rewire fails, your instinct is to *try harder tomorrow*. This is paying willpower tax to compensate for bad design. Willpower is finite and unreliable; environment is permanent.

**If you have failed the same habit 3 times, the bug is the environment, not you.** Stop paying the tax; rebuild the design.

blocks.prompt: You want to install 'one glass of water as soon as I wake up.' Order the steps from highest to lowest leverage:

items.label: Place a glass + filled bottle on bedside table the night before
items.detail: Friction reduction at the moment of cue — single highest leverage move.

items.label: Anchor the cue: 'phone alarm off → reach for glass'
items.detail: Without an explicit cue the chain never starts; second highest leverage.

items.label: Tick a small visible calendar box for the streak
items.detail: Accountability + log; mid leverage, but compounds.

items.label: Resolve to drink 2 litres immediately and feel virtuous
items.detail: Largest first step; lowest leverage — sets you up to fail and then quit.

blocks.instruction: Take one habit you have repeatedly failed to install. Specify the cue, the friction reduction, the tiny first step, and the accountability mechanism. Be embarrassingly specific.
blocks.expected:
Example — 'I want to journal at night.'
1. Cue: right after I plug in my phone to charge at 10:45 pm.
2. Friction: notebook + pen kept on the charging pad. Same notebook, no system shopping.
3. Tiny first step: write one sentence. Even 'today was fine.' That counts.
4. Accountability: text one friend a 👍 emoji each night I do it; nothing if I skip. Ten skips and they call me.

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO most defensible reasons a previously failed habit will succeed this time using the 4-part rewire:

choices.label: It removes 2-3 specific points of friction that previously killed the chain
choices.explain: Correct. Friction is usually the single biggest predictor of habit survival.

choices.label: It uses a known cue instead of a vague intention
choices.explain: Correct. Cues bypass the planner-vs-doer translation entirely.

choices.label: You will be more motivated this time
choices.explain: This is the willpower tax. Motivation is precisely what the rewire is designed to *not* depend on.

choices.label: The behavior is now larger and more meaningful
choices.explain: Inverse of the truth. Larger goals fail faster; the rewire works by shrinking step one until it cannot fail.

hi-IN.title: Indian household ki accountability — natural friction
hi-IN.md:
Tu kabhi notice kiya: ghar pe rehne par tu apne aap subah uthta hai. Mummy 6 baje uthi, kitchen mein cup ki awaaz, papa news dekh rahe hain — *cue is loud and external.*

Flat mein akela rehne par cue zero ho jaata hai. Phone alarm sirf snooze ka button ban jaata hai.

Matlab? Tu lazy nahi hai. Tu under-cued hai. Wapas environment design kar — alarm room ke door se baahar rakh, bedmate (real ya virtual) ko text bhej. Mummy ka kitchen replicate kar.

en.title: Why you wake up earlier at home
en.md: Live alone: you sleep till 9, fight your alarm. Live with family: somehow you're up at 6:30, no alarm needed. You aren't more disciplined at home. The environment is. The cues are loud, social, and constant. Replicate that and you will too.

blocks.title: Field Notes: Nine Years of Knowing About Sleep
blocks.source: A senior backend developer in Koramangala, Bengaluru (told over chai, anonymised)
blocks.story:
Karthik, 38, has been a Staff Engineer at a payments company since 2017. He has read *Why We Sleep* twice. He owns an Oura ring (since 2019), an 8Sleep mattress cover (since 2022), and has subscribed to 4 different sleep podcasts. His Notion has a 'Sleep Protocol' page last updated 11 February 2024. He can quote the cortisol-melatonin curve from memory.

For 9 years and 2 months, he has checked work email at 6:58 a.m. from bed. Every single day. He knows the email check spikes his cortisol by ~40 percent within 8 minutes, kills the morning sunlight ritual he has also read about, and explains 80 percent of his afternoon crashes. He has a Whoop screenshot proving the pattern. He has shown me the screenshot on three separate visits.

He came to me because his wife, Divya, finally asked: 'You've spent ₹2.4 lakh on sleep tech and zero rupees on actually moving the phone out of the bedroom. Why?'

This is the G.I. Joe fallacy in its purest form: knowing IS NOT half the battle. Knowing is roughly 4 percent of the battle. The other 96 percent is friction design — and Karthik had aggressively engineered the *opposite*: bedside charger, work email pinned to home screen, Slack notifications on. The phone moved 1.2 metres on the day he fixed it. Email-check rate: from 1.0 per day to 0.07.
blocks.takeaway: If you've known a thing for 9 years and not done it, you don't have a knowledge problem. You have a friction problem. Move the object, not the mind.

blocks.title: Aarav vs the Evening Walk
blocks.setup:
Aarav, riding the high of his hedonic-adaptation experiment, decided 4 weeks ago to add an 'evening walk, 6:30 p.m., 25 mins' to his routine. He's read the lesson. He knows about the 4 rewire parts: **cue, friction, accountability, identity**.

Voice note:

> *bro I have FAILED. 4 weeks, 6 walks. SIX. and I know everything from the lesson, I literally have it bookmarked. tell me what's broken.*

You just finished Lesson 3. Diagnose which of the 4 parts is missing.

stages.prompt: You ask Aarav to describe his current setup. He says: 'I just plan to walk at 6:30. I check my watch around then, and if a meeting overruns or Meera's making chai, I skip.' First diagnosis?

options.label: He's lazy. Willpower problem.
options.explain: 'Lazy' is the diagnosis people reach for when they haven't read the lesson. Tarini will not accept this. Try again.

options.label: Missing **cue**: 'around 6:30' isn't a cue, it's a rough wish. He needs an environmental trigger — phone alarm + shoes by the door + a visual anchor like 'when the building lights come on'.
options.explain: Exactly. A vague time isn't a cue. Cues are concrete, environmental, and impossible to miss. Lesson 3 was unambiguous about this.

options.label: Missing **identity**: he doesn't think of himself as 'a walker' yet.
options.explain: Possibly true but you're skipping the obvious mechanical failure. Identity comes after a few reps land. Right now no rep is even firing.

options.label: Missing **accountability**: he needs a walking buddy.
options.explain: Accountability is a real lever but it doesn't fix the fact that the trigger to start the walk doesn't exist in the first place.

stages.prompt: Aarav adds a 6:30 alarm + shoes by the door. Walks 4 of next 7 days. Better but he says: 'On meeting-heavy days I see the alarm, dismiss it, tell myself I'll go after one more email. Never go.' What's still broken?

options.label: **Friction is wrong direction**: skipping the walk has lower friction than doing it. He needs to RAISE the cost of skipping (e.g. ₹500 to a friend's UPI per skip via stickK or manual).
options.explain: When the cost of skipping = 0 and the cost of going = 25 minutes + bothering Meera, the math always wins for skipping. Adding a financial sting flips the equation. This is the asymmetry the lesson called out.

options.label: Push the walk to morning instead.
options.explain: Time-shifting doesn't fix the underlying issue: he hasn't built any friction *against* skipping. Same problem will reappear at 7 a.m.

options.label: Drop walks, try a different habit.
options.explain: He's failing the system, not the habit. Switching habits without fixing the rewire parts will produce the same failure on a new noun.

options.label: Add a second alarm.
options.explain: He's not missing the alarm. He's choosing to dismiss it. More alarms = more dismissals.

stages.prompt: Aarav adds a ₹500-per-skip rule (paid to his cousin Rohan). Walks 6 of next 7 days. He's thrilled. He asks: 'Should I add the identity move now? Start calling myself a walker?'

options.label: No. He has 6 reps. He needs ~30 reps before identity sticks. Premature identity-claiming feels fake and collapses on the first miss.
options.explain: Lesson 3 was specific: identity is the *output* of consistent behaviour, not the input. Claiming 'I'm a walker' at rep 6 is the LinkedIn-bio version of habit formation.

options.label: Yes, manifest it now, identity drives behaviour.
options.explain: Cute on Instagram, wrong in the lesson. Identity-first is what 12-month-old failed gym memberships are made of.

options.label: Add accountability instead — group chat with 3 friends.
options.explain: He already has accountability via Rohan and the ₹500 rule. Stacking another layer is over-engineering. Let the current system bake.

options.label: Drop the ₹500 rule, walk should be intrinsic now.
options.explain: Removing the friction at rep 6 will collapse the habit. Intrinsic motivation comes around rep 60-ish, not rep 6.

stages.prompt: Final move. Aarav, 6 walks deep, asks: 'What's the marker for when I CAN drop the ₹500 rule?'

options.label: When he goes 21 consecutive days without skipping AND has caught himself walking on auto-pilot at least 3 times (cue fires, body moves, no internal debate).
options.explain: Two-criteria gate: streak (proves the system works) + auto-pilot reps (proves the cue is wired). This is exactly the de-scaffolding test the lesson recommended. Tarini approves.

options.label: After 1 month, automatically.
options.explain: Calendar-based de-scaffolding ignores actual evidence of habit strength. A bad month and a great month are not the same data.

options.label: When walks 'feel natural'.
options.explain: 'Feels natural' is a vibe, not a marker. Lesson explicitly warned against vibe-based progress measurement.

options.label: Never drop it, friction is forever.
options.explain: Permanent ₹500 stakes are unsustainable and miss the point. The friction is scaffolding; you remove scaffolding when the structure stands.

outcomes.perfect: 12/12. You diagnosed cue then friction then resisted both premature identity-claiming and premature de-scaffolding. Aarav now has a working evening-walk system. Tarini sends a rare 'beta, well done' from Pune.
outcomes.good: 8-11. You found the right rewire parts but tripped on sequencing. The lesson's ordering — cue, then friction, then identity — exists for a reason.
outcomes.learn: Under 8. You either reached for 'try harder' or skipped to identity-mode. The G.I. Joe fallacy is alive in your diagnosis. Re-read the 4 rewire parts.

points: Knowing is roughly 10% of the battle; the cartoon was wrong about the ratio
Behavior change has 4 parts: cue, friction reduction, tiny step, accountability
If you have failed a habit 3 times, the bug is the environment, not you
Willpower is a tax; environment is a permanent rebate
Most failures are missing only one of the four parts — diagnose, don't restart

audioChapters.label: Opening — the index funds of well-being

blocks.md:
If lessons one and two told you what does *not* work (most external upgrades), this lesson tells you the two things that show up in nearly every well-being meta-analysis. They are unsexy, free, and almost everyone underweights them. Convenient.

We will run gratitude first, then connection — and you will leave with a *specific* template for each that you can run this Sunday.

blocks.title: Mental model: well-being is a portfolio
blocks.md:
Think of well-being like a stock portfolio. External upgrades (salary, gadgets, that flat with the balcony) are individual stocks — high variance, often disappointing. Gratitude and social connection are *index funds* — low excitement, absurdly good long-term returns, and almost no one allocates enough to them.

**Most people allocate 95% to individual stocks.** This lesson is about rebalancing.

hi-IN.title: Naani ki diary — original gratitude practice
hi-IN.md:
Naani har Sunday ko ek choti diary kholti thi. Pen pakad ke teen line likhti — "aaj Bittu ne phone kiya, doctor ne report theek bola, kal sambhar acha bana." Bas. Sunday ka Sunday.

Woh research nahi padhi thi. Woh Emmons & McCullough ki paper nahi padhi thi. Naani 1972 mein already running the protocol that the labs would prove in 2003. **Specific, weekly, causal — naani knew.**

en.title: Grandmothers ran this protocol decades before the labs
en.md: The exact gratitude protocol that won in the Emmons & McCullough study — specific, weekly, causal — has been running in your grandmother's notebook for 40 years. The labs caught up; she was already there.

blocks.md:
*"Just be grateful, bro"* is exactly as useful as *"just be confident, bro."* The science is on **structured** gratitude: specific, written, novel each entry, with a cause attached.

Emmons & McCullough's classic protocol: **3 things, once a week, with cause attached, for 10 weeks** beat both daily journaling and a control on subjective well-being. The weekly cadence outperformed daily — daily produced too much repetition; the brain adapted to gratitude itself.

A bad entry: *"I am grateful for my health."* A good entry: *"I am grateful that my back held up during the 4 km walk on Tuesday morning, because I have done the strength work consistently for three weeks."* **Specific, novel, causal.**

coach.name: Naani's Notes
coach.role: Reads your gratitude entry and tells you, calmly, whether it counts.

intro: Main har entry padhungi aur batti dungi — **strong** (specific, novel, causal), **weak** (vague or repeat), ya **wrong cadence** (right content, wrong frequency). Sirf strong entries thermostat hilate hain.

scenarios.situation: Sunday entry: 'Grateful for my parents and my health.'
scenarios.explain: Vague. No what, no when, no cause. The brain registers nothing. Better: 'Grateful that Mummy called Saturday morning to ask about my cold, because I had texted her on Wednesday — the cadence we agreed on is starting to hold.'

scenarios.situation: Sunday entry: 'Grateful that the team didn't drop the ball on Friday's release, because I spent Wednesday doing the runbook walk-through with everyone instead of writing it alone.'
scenarios.explain: Strong. Specific (Friday's release), novel (this week), causal (Wednesday walk-through). This is the form that moves the numbers.

scenarios.situation: Daily journal, day 47: 'Grateful for my girlfriend.'
scenarios.explain: Wrong cadence. Daily produces over-adaptation; you've already adapted to gratitude itself. Switch to weekly, force novelty per entry.

scenarios.situation: Sunday entry: 'Grateful that my landlord renewed at the same rent, because I had paid on time every month and asked early in writing.'
scenarios.explain: Strong. Specific, novel for this week, causal. The cause attaches gratitude to *your own behavior*, which compounds over weeks.

scenarios.situation: Sunday entry copied from last Sunday: 'Grateful for sunshine, food, family.'
scenarios.explain: Vague AND repeated. Two failure modes at once. The brain pattern-matches and discards.

blocks.prompt: Why does Emmons & McCullough's *weekly* gratitude practice outperform a *daily* one?

choices.label: Daily is too frequent; the brain adapts to gratitude itself, and entries lose novelty
choices.explain: Correct. Hedonic adaptation applies even to gratitude practice. Weekly forces novelty per entry.

choices.label: Daily journaling is dramatically better than weekly
choices.explain: Tempting because more = more, right? Not here. Gratitude is one of the few well-being moves where less is more.

choices.label: Journaling has no measurable effect
choices.explain: Did not read; the entire study found a measurable effect.

choices.label: Only group journaling produces effects
choices.explain: Not what the study tested. Solo, written, weekly was enough.

hi-IN.title: WhatsApp ke 'good morning' forwards = gratitude ka opposite
hi-IN.md:
Tu daily 'have a great day' forward kar raha hai 14 logon ko. Kuch nahi ho raha — na tujhe, na unhe. Brain has fully adapted; flowers ke GIFs are wallpaper at this point.

Uske badle, ek Sunday ko ek banda pick kar. Ek paragraph likh — *specific, novel, causal*. "Aarav, last week tune meri presentation se pehle 30 min nikaal ke practice karwaayi, jiski wajah se main nervously baat nahi kara — thanks bhai."

Forward count: 14 → 1. Impact: 0 → measurable.

en.title: The WhatsApp forward fallacy
en.md: Sending 14 'have a great day' forwards every morning is gratitude theater, not gratitude. The receivers register nothing; you register nothing. Replace it with one specific message to one specific person about a specific thing they did. Quantity zero, signal high.

blocks.md:
The Harvard Study of Adult Development is the longest study of human happiness ever run — 80+ years, two cohorts, more data than any single researcher really wanted. The headline: at age 50, the strength of close relationships predicts physical and mental health at age 80 better than cholesterol does.

And yet most adults treat friendships as something that *happens*, not something they *engineer*. By age 30, the average person's deep friendships are decaying at roughly 1 to 2 per year unless actively maintained.

The word that does the work in this section is **engineered**.

blocks.title: What 'engineering' a friendship actually looks like over 4 weeks

steps.label: Week 1 — The audit
steps.body: List 5 people you would call at 11 pm if something went wrong. If you cannot list 5, start there. This is not depressing; it is information.

steps.label: Week 2 — The opener
steps.body: Send one no-agenda message to someone you have not spoken to in 6+ months. Specifically: a memory, not a 'hey how are you.'

steps.label: Week 3 — The cadence
steps.body: Schedule one recurring slot — Tuesday 8 pm call with one person, monthly walk with another. Cadence beats spontaneity, every time.

steps.label: Week 4 — The depth move
steps.body: On one of these calls, share something *currently uncertain* in your life. Vulnerability is the only known accelerator of closeness, and it is annoyingly safe over voice.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the spontaneity myth
blocks.md:
Adults love saying *"we should catch up sometime."* Sometime is not a date. Sometime is a polite, mutual lie. If you do not put a slot on the calendar, the friendship is on a glide-path to acquaintance.

**Calendar > intention, every single time.** This is one of the few rules in this course with no exceptions.

blocks.prompt: Order these social moves from highest to lowest expected return on well-being, based on the literature:

items.label: Schedule a recurring weekly slot with one person you trust
items.detail: Highest signal — cadence, depth, low friction.

items.label: Send a no-agenda 'I was thinking of you because…' message
items.detail: Medium-high; restarts dormant relationships at almost zero cost.

items.label: Attend an event with 30+ acquaintances
items.detail: Mild positive bump; acquaintance density helps but doesn't substitute for depth.

items.label: Like someone's post and consider the friendship maintained
items.detail: Net zero or negative; gives the planner a sense of action without producing any.

blocks.instruction: Pick one specific person. Write the exact message you will send them today, AND the exact recurring slot you will propose. No vague 'sometime soon.'
blocks.expected: Example: 'Hey Ananya, I was thinking about that disastrous trek where you sprained your ankle on the second km. Are you free for a 30-minute call on Tuesdays at 8:30 pm? I would like to make it a thing — even if half the calls are just venting about work.'

blocks.prompt: What is the most defensible interpretation of the Harvard Study's headline finding?

choices.label: At age 50, the strength of close relationships predicts physical health at 80 better than cholesterol does
choices.explain: Correct. The cholesterol comparison is what made the study famous.

choices.label: Income is the strongest predictor of long-run health
choices.explain: Income matters, mostly below a threshold; above it, relationships dominate the long-run model.

choices.label: Exercise is the dominant predictor
choices.explain: Useful, but did not lead the model in the long-run prediction.

choices.label: The study found no relationship between connection and health
choices.explain: Inverse of the actual finding.

hi-IN.title: 'Bhai, milte hain' = polite jhoot — confess kar
hi-IN.md:
Last 5 saal mein "yaar milte hain jaldi" kitni baar bola? 200? 400? Kitne actual mein mile?

Dekha?

"Milte hain" ek sentence hai jo dono log bolte hain knowing it won't happen, kyunki actual proposal awkward lagta hai. Iska fix bhi awkward hai: **"Tuesday raat 8:30 baje free hai? 30 min ki call?" Period.**

Doosra banda ya haan bolega ya na — dono cases mein sometime se zyada concrete data tujhe mil gaya.

en.title: 'Let's catch up sometime' is a mutual lie
en.md: Count how many times you've said 'let's catch up' in the last five years vs how many times you actually have. The phrase is a polite social lubricant, not a plan. Replace it with a specific time slot. Yes it's awkward. Yes it works.

blocks.title: Field Notes: A Tuesday Phone Call, +1.5 Ladder Points
blocks.source: A 34-year-old infrastructure engineer in Whitefield, Bengaluru (writeup shared on a closed Slack of ex-colleagues, used with permission)
blocks.story:
Pranav, 34, runs a 9-person SRE team. After a divorce in 2023 his social graph collapsed to: wife of best friend (awkward), 2 cousins (functional), one running buddy who moved to Berlin in early 2024.

In July 2025 he ran one experiment, taken from a podcast he half-remembered: he texted Suresh, his closest friend from a 2014 startup, and proposed a recurring video call every Tuesday at 9 p.m. IST, no agenda, 30 minutes minimum, 90 max. Both opted in. The rule: it happens unless one of them is on a flight or in surgery.

He tracked his Cantril ladder weekly on a Google Sheet starting July 7. Baseline: 5.8.

- Week 1-3: 5.9, 5.8, 6.1 (no real movement, calls felt forced)
- Week 4-6: 6.4, 6.6, 6.5 (the 'depth threshold' kicked in around call 4 — they started talking about real things, not work)
- Week 7-12: 6.9, 7.0, 7.2, 7.1, 7.3, 7.3 (steady, sticky)
- Week 13: 7.3

Net movement: +1.5 ladder points over 13 weeks. He spent ₹0. He gained ~6 hours of conversation. The Whoop data showed a parallel ~9 percent improvement in sleep variability on Tuesday nights.

Most telling: he told me 'I underestimated this by an order of magnitude. I would have paid ₹50,000 to feel this much better and spent it on a fitness coach instead.'
blocks.takeaway: One scheduled, no-agenda, depth-friendly call with one real person, weekly, beats most things you can buy. Cadence and depth matter more than headcount.

blocks.title: Aarav's Drifting Four
blocks.setup:
Mid-week voice note from Aarav, six days into his first gratitude+connection sprint:

> *yaar, I did the friend audit. four people I actually care about — Rohan (cousin, Pune), Suresh (college, now in Bangalore but we haven't met in 8 months), Priya (ex-teammate, Hyderabad), and Akshay (school friend, in the same city, drifted hard). I have ONE WEEK to sequence the moves before this momentum dies. Walk me through it, lesson 4 style.*

You just finished Lesson 4. Help him pick the audit / opener / cadence / depth-move sequence.

stages.prompt: Aarav already did the audit (4 names). What's the next move per the lesson?

options.label: Send all 4 a long heartfelt text right now.
options.explain: Mass-firing a vulnerability blast is a great way to feel exposed and get 1 reply. Lesson 4 sequenced opener BEFORE depth for a reason.

options.label: Pick the lowest-friction opener for each person — one short, specific, no-pressure ping referencing a real shared memory or current life event. Cast 4, see what comes back.
options.explain: Openers are deliberately low-stakes: a meme, a song, 'saw this and thought of you'. The job of the opener is to restart the channel, not to deliver depth. The lesson called this the 'reconnect probe'.

options.label: Wait for them to text first.
options.explain: Drift gets fixed by the person who notices the drift. Waiting is the documented pattern that produced the drift in the first place.

options.label: Add them all to a group chat.
options.explain: Group chats are where 1:1 friendships go to die. The lesson was explicit: depth lives in 1:1 channels.

stages.prompt: Three of four reply within 48 hours. Akshay (the same-city drifted friend) ghosts. What does Aarav do with the 3 who replied?

options.label: Move all 3 to weekly calls immediately.
options.explain: Weekly is the right cadence for the relationship that *fits* it (one person, like Pranav-Suresh in the field notes). Three weeklies is a load that will crash by week 4.

options.label: Pick ONE for a recurring weekly call (Suresh, lives in same city, easiest), and set monthly cadence for Rohan and Priya. One channel-per-friend, matched to feasibility.
options.explain: This is the cadence-matching move from the lesson. One depth relationship + two warm relationships > three forced weeklies. Pranav's field notes are the proof: one weekly call moved his ladder 1.5 points.

options.label: Skip cadence, just message them when he feels like it.
options.explain: Cadence-by-feeling is how the original drift happened. The lesson was unambiguous: connection requires *scheduled* recurrence.

options.label: Pick the one he's most romantically drawn to talk to.
options.explain: Aarav is engaged. This is a different kind of trap, not the lesson's trap. Skip.

stages.prompt: Suresh agrees to a weekly Tuesday 9 p.m. call. Call 1 happens, lasts 22 minutes, mostly cricket. Aarav says: 'felt nice but not deep, am I doing it wrong?'

options.label: Call it off, find a different friend.
options.explain: Call 1 is supposed to feel surface-level. Pranav's data showed depth kicked in around call 4. Quitting at call 1 is the impatience trap the lesson named.

options.label: Trust the depth threshold. Run 4-5 calls before judging. Add ONE depth-move to call 3: 'what's something you've been chewing on that you haven't told anyone?'
options.explain: Cricket-level rapport is the runway, not the destination. The depth-move at call 3 is the lesson's 'open one door' technique — small, optional, not a confession demand.

options.label: Skip cricket, jump to deep questions on call 2.
options.explain: Forcing depth before the channel is warm reads as therapy ambush. The depth-move works *because* the channel is comfortable first.

options.label: Add a third person to the call to make it more interesting.
options.explain: Adding a third caps depth at the lowest common comfort. 1:1 stays 1:1. The lesson was loud about this.

stages.prompt: What does Aarav do about Akshay (the ghoster)?

options.label: Send 4 follow-ups across 2 weeks.
options.explain: Pestering converts 'drifted' into 'actively avoided'. The opener is one shot.

options.label: One follow-up after 10-14 days with a different specific hook (concert, restaurant, mutual friend's news). If still silent, archive the relationship — not forever, just not in this sprint.
options.explain: Two openers max. After that, the relationship goes into the 'warm acquaintance' bucket. The lesson was clear that not every reconnect lands, and chasing is worse than archiving.

options.label: Show up at his house unannounced.
options.explain: Bold. Also a great way to find out exactly why he ghosted.

options.label: Take it personally and unfollow him on everything.
options.explain: Burning the bridge is the over-correction trap. Akshay might just be in a bad month.

outcomes.perfect: 12/12. You ran audit then opener then matched cadence then trusted the depth threshold and handled the ghoster cleanly. Aarav now has a 1-weekly + 2-monthly social system that costs him ₹0. Tarini sends actual praise from Pune.
outcomes.good: 8-11. Right shape, wrong sequencing in places. The lesson's order — opener, cadence, depth-move — is load-bearing.
outcomes.learn: Under 8. You either over-fired the openers or rushed depth. Re-read the cadence-matching section; the answer is rarely 'message everyone weekly'.

points: Gratitude works when it is specific, novel, causal, and weekly — not vague and daily
Close relationships at 50 predict health at 80 better than cholesterol does
Adult friendships decay 1 to 2 per year on default settings; you have to engineer the maintenance
"We should catch up sometime" is a polite, mutual lie until it lands on a calendar
Vulnerability is the only known accelerator of closeness and is surprisingly safe over voice

audioChapters.label: Opening — track everything except the variable that matters

blocks.md:
You track your weight. You probably track your steps. You almost certainly track your portfolio. You don't track the one variable everything else is allegedly serving.

This is the lesson where we fix that, with the same rigor and roughly the same effort. Two minutes a week. Three numbers. One 14-day loop. Done.

blocks.title: Mental model: just-enough observability
blocks.md:
Treat your well-being like a small, well-instrumented system. You don't need a dashboard with 40 metrics; you need 3 numbers, captured cheaply, looked at weekly.

Engineers call this *just-enough observability*. Therapists call it *self-monitoring*. Same idea, different priesthood.

**Anything past three numbers is procrastination dressed as instrumentation.**

hi-IN.title: Notion dashboard ka shraadh — har techie ka guilty secret
hi-IN.md:
Saturday raat 11 baje. Tu Notion mein 22-widget dashboard banaya — mood emoji column, weekly graph, color-coded sleep bar, 4 templates from YouTube. Bahut santosh hua.

Monday: ek baar dekha.

Wednesday: "yaar update karna hai dashboard" — nahi kiya.

Friday: bhool gaya kahaan tha.

Mahine baad: link bhi kho gaya.

**Yeh procrastination ko productive lagne wala dress pehnaya gaya hai.** 3 numbers, ek note app, Sunday 9 baje. Bas. Iss se zyada engineering teri zindagi ka time kha rahi hai.

en.title: The dashboard delusion
en.md: Building the elaborate tracker is the part that feels productive. Maintaining it is the part that doesn't get done. Three numbers in a plain note will outperform a 22-widget Notion setup, every time, because the second one mostly gets abandoned.

blocks.md:
There are exactly three numbers worth tracking weekly. Skip any of them and you will misdiagnose yourself.

1. **PANAS-short** — 10 emotions, rate 1 to 5. Captures both positive *and* negative affect (it turns out they are not opposites — you can be high on both, or low on both).
2. **Cantril ladder** — "On a 0 to 10 ladder where 10 is the best possible life for you, where do you stand today?" Single integer. The Gallup World Poll uses this; comparable across years.
3. **Sleep hours, last night** — the highest-correlation single behavioral input to next-day affect. Boring, decisive.

Log these once a week, same day, same time. That's it. Two minutes.

blocks.prompt: Why does the PANAS measure positive AND negative affect separately, instead of one happiness score?

choices.label: Because positive and negative affect are partly independent — you can score high on both, or low on both
choices.explain: Correct. Two separate axes capture states a single 0–10 score collapses (e.g. 'busy and stimulated but anxious' vs 'flat and calm').

choices.label: Because researchers like long forms
choices.explain: Tempting cynicism, but no — the dual-axis design is empirically driven, not procedural.

choices.label: Because positive emotions are not real
choices.explain: Did not read. The form treats both as equally real.

choices.label: Because negative emotions are weighted more
choices.explain: Not the design. Both axes are scored on equal scales.

hi-IN.title: PANAS ke 'busy + anxious' quadrant ka naam: corporate Bharat
hi-IN.md:
Software engineer. Salary acchi. Sprint mein deliver ho raha hai. Manager khush. *PANAS positive: 17* (excited about launch, alert about prod, interested in new feature).

Lekin Sunday raat ko anxiety: *PANAS negative: 18* (sleep aage ki sprint ka, scared of next quarter, jittery about RSU vesting).

Single score "happy ya not happy?" puchhe toh tu confuse ho jaayega. Dual axis bole, **"bro tu busy + anxious quadrant mein hai. Both numbers high. Ye corporate Bharat ka modal point hai. Bohot log waha hain. Calm + low quadrant mein jaane ka rasta hai, lekin pehle pehchan toh."**

en.title: Why your single 'happy?' answer is misleading
en.md: Asked 'how happy are you?' on a single 0-10 scale, you'll average your stimulating week with your anxious Sundays and produce a meaningless 7. Asked separately, 'positive 17 / negative 18' tells you exactly which lever to pull. Information per question matters.

blocks.md:
Tracking is necessary; tracking alone is not the experiment. The experiment is: pick one intervention from this course, run it for 14 days, compare your check-in numbers before and after.

Good interventions to test (each isolates one variable):
- *Variety swap*: rotate 3 different morning routines for 14 days vs a fixed one.
- *Weekly gratitude*: 3 specific entries every Sunday for two Sundays.
- *One engineered friendship slot*: a recurring 30-minute call.
- *Sleep floor*: hard rule, 7+ hours, every night, no exceptions.

One intervention, 14 days, three numbers before, three numbers after. **That's the entire scientific method, in a tracksuit.**

blocks.title: The classic trap: the dashboard delusion
blocks.md:
You can spend a fun weekend building a Notion dashboard with 22 metrics, automated graphs, and a mood emoji column. You will check it twice and then never again.

**Three numbers, once a week, in a plain note.** Anything fancier is procrastination dressed as instrumentation. The fanciness is the whole bug.
